links.passage: The benefits of drip irrigation compared to conventional irrigation in Indian pomegranate orchards included c. 42 % increased yield and c. 38 % higher net returns for farmers in the Kullu district in Himachal Pradesh (Singh and Sharma, 2013).

According to Kumar et al. (2013) use of an auxiliary reservoir in combination with drip irrigation saved a substantial amount of irrigation water (c. 32 %) compared to surface methods in an arid Punjab region.

In comparison to surface irrigation systems drip irrigation increased pomegranate irrigation water productivity in the Punjab region by 82 % (5.32 kg m−3) while net profit per mm water applied almost doubled for drip irrigation (Kumar et al., 2013).
Frequent drip irrigation furthermore limited variation in soil water availability and decreased pomegranate fruit cracking by 10–15 %, which increased marketable yield.
supporting_passages: In comparison to surface irrigation systems drip irrigation increased pomegranate irrigation water productivity in the Punjab region by 82 % (5.32 kg m−3) while net profit per mm water applied almost doubled for drip irrigation (Kumar et al., 2013).
links.inference_note: The claim that drip reduced fruit cracking and increased marketable yield continues the discussion of the Kumar et al. (2013) study cited in the preceding sentences.

links.passage: Ghosh et al. (2013) also found that drip irrigated plants had less fruit cracking than basin irrigated plants.

Further potential advantages of drip irrigation over the conventional methods (i.e. flood, furrow, ring basin) include a saving of up to 50 % of water; lower labour costs related to weed control and application of fertilizers and pesticides, and better control over water application on sloping terrain and variable soils (Singh and Sharma, 2013).

Benefits of well managed surface drip and subsurface drip irrigation systems include eliminated or reduced runoff and deep drainage, minimized surface soil and plant evaporation, reduced transpiration of drought tolerant crops and reduced fertilizer losses (Ayars et al., 1999).

Subsurface compared to surface drip irrigation on a sandy loam soil in California resulted in a significant increase in yield of prime (good colour, diameter >80 mm, minimal cracking with no open cracks) and/or subprime (suitable for juice, green, open cracked) fruit for some years (Ayars et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2015).

links.passage: Use of subsurface drip irrigation resulted in reduced weed pressure compared to surface drip irrigation.
supporting_passages: Total yield was consistently higher in the subsurface compared to surface drip system, but due to an additional 10 % water being applied to the surface drip irrigation treatment to compensate for evaporative water loss and weed growth, not significantly different (Ayars et al., 2017).
links.inference_note: The reduced weed pressure statement continues the account of the Ayars et al. (2017) subsurface versus surface drip comparison cited in the preceding sentence.

links.passage: These include: wetting pattern issues on coarse soils; difficulties in monitoring and evaluation of system operation and application efficiency; emitter discharge rates and water redistribution disparities, restricted plant root development and its role in irrigation and fertilization and crop water stresses even when the root zone is well watered.
supporting_passages: Although subsurface drip irrigation systems have advantages, there are also some disadvantages to take into account (Lamm, 2002).
links.inference_note: The preceding sentence names subsurface drip and carries the Lamm (2002) citation, while the listed disadvantages state restricted root development and crop water stress as harms.
